 CNN panel discusses Vance blaming midterm performance on Iran war 
 6:32
 Vice President JD Vance took to social media today to deliver his post-mortem on Republicans’ grim performance in the midterms, making clear that he thought one factor deserved the most blame: “The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote.
 Some observers immediately read Vance’s statement as a move to set himself up for a 2028 presidential run – but whether he has a realistic chance after last night is unclear, CNN reporters and contributors said on a panel after Vance posted his comments.
 “ I think the biggest single loser last night was JD Vance,” CNN political commentator Jonah Goldberg said. “Because he is Donald Trump with twice the bigotry and half the charm. And that is not what the country said they want more of for the next two years, never mind the next six.”
 Lulu Garcia-Navarro, a CNN contributor and New York Times journalist, was even more blunt. “This is the death knell for JD Vance, his political aspirations for 2028,” she said.
 Leading up to the election, Vance focused much of his attention on launching personal attacks against Democratic candidates and turning the discussion to culture war issues, CNN chief national affairs correspondent Jeff Zeleny noted. His change of tone now is unlikely to convince voters in 2028, members of the panel argued.
 “The party has never loved him. He has been on all sides of every issue here,” Zeleny said. “So this is his trying to reset for 2028. The people in Ted Cruz world and other Republicans out there are going to eat his lunch if he decides to be a primary candidate.”

 Republican source says blue wave in the Tar Heel state is "a bloodbath"
 By Lauren Kent and Dianne Gallagher 
 Democrat senatorial candidate Roy Cooper greets supporters during an election night event in Raleigh, North Carolina on Tuesday. 
 A.M Stewart/AFP/Getty Images 
 The blue wave rippled from coastal North Carolina to the Appalachian Mountains on Tuesday, with Democrats flipping at least two House seats, while leading in several other races that CNN has yet to project.
 “A blue tsunami from Manteo to Murphy. It’s a bloodbath for us,” one high-level Republican operative told CNN late Tuesday night.
 In western North Carolina, Democratic candidate and local farmer Jamie Ager pulled off a shocking seat-flip in a congressional district that President Donald Trump once carried by 10 points. Notably, incumbent Democratic Rep. Don Davis is also projected to retain the 1st District , which state Republicans redistricted to produce an area that Trump carried by more than 11 points.
 “Davis won because several things lined up: incumbency, a moderate profile that blunted attacks, an off-cycle redistricting fight that he turned to his advantage, and a Democratic wave strong enough to carry him through a district less favorable to his party,” said political scientist Daniel DiSalvo, a professor at the University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill.
 Meanwhile, in a major flip, Richard Hudson, chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee, is projected to lose his NC-9 House seat. And longtime Congresswoman Virginia Foxx is at risk of losing the seat she’s held since 2005, although that race is still too close to call .
 Asked if the apparent popularity of Democratic Senate candidate Roy Cooper – who CNN projects will win the Senate seat with nearly 59% of the vote – contributed to the success of down-ballot candidates, DiSalvo said it “certainly didn’t hurt.”
“But (it) probably didn’t make that much of a difference. These races were driven either by large national trends – Trump’s unpopularity and the economy – or very localized factors,” the UNC professor told CNN. “That said, Cooper ran a model campaign that projected a moderate, steady image.”

 “We have a state to save, now more than ever,” Rogers says after Michigan Senate loss
 By Maureen Chowdhury , Nicky Robertson and Sunlen Serfaty 
 Republican Mike Rogers arrives for a midterm election night watch party at the Westin Book Cadillac Detroit hotel on Tuesday in Detroit. 
 Spencer Platt/Getty Images 
 Republican Mike Rogers said, “We have a state to save, now more than ever,” in a statement following his projected loss to Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the state’s Senate race.
 Rogers reflected on his campaign in the statement: “Over the past two years, Kristi and I have met incredible Michiganders who want solutions, not division. We’ve worked to put a spotlight on literacy, affordable housing, manufacturing jobs, Detroit’s food desert, and the troubling rise of antisemitism.”
 “We will be forever grateful to the families, faith leaders, and community leaders who welcomed us. We focused on what brings us together — and on real solutions to the real issues that Michiganders face,” he said in the statement, which does not mention El-Sayed.
 “Michigan — we have a state to save, now more than ever. Our work continues, and I remain hopeful that Michigan’s best days are ahead,” Rogers wrote at the close of his statement.
 The statement does not explicitly concede the race.
 A senior Republican official did not think it was likely that Rogers would make a concession call.

 Mississippi Democrat says he's "confident" he'll win razor-thin Senate race 
 0:55
 Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom expressed confidence Wednesday that he would win a razor-thin race for Senate, vowing to ensure that all of the state’s ballots are counted in the coming days.
 “I’m confident once the process plays out, where we are, where the ballots are, we’re gonna win,” he said during a news conference. “And it’s because the people of Mississippi turned out in historic numbers to make this race possible in a midterm election.”
 Colom’s remarks came as he holds a lead over Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith of fewer than 100 votes. If he prevails, it would represent one of the biggest upsets in a midterm wave that’s ushered Democrats into office in traditionally GOP strongholds across the nation.
 “Unlike all the people across the country that might be surprised, our campaign, our volunteers, the people of Mississippi, are not surprised,” Colom said, adding that his team will work to “protect the process of this election.”
 Asked for his reaction to Hyde-Smith’s own statement’s declaring that she expected to win the race, Colom would only say: “Bless her heart.”

 Donald Trump Jr. endorses Vance's assessment that Iran is to blame for GOP losses
 By Kevin Liptak 
 Donald Trump Jr., speaks at the Republican convention on September 10, in Dallas. 
 Alex Brandon/AP 
 Donald Trump Jr., the president’s eldest son, endorsed the conclusion reached by Vice President JD Vance that the Iran war was responsible for Republicans’ historic midterm losses.
 “Every word of this,” the president’s son wrote atop Vance’s 620-word post assigning blame on the Middle East conflict for Tuesday’s electoral defeat.
 That put two of the most critical figures in Trump’s orbit on the record saying the war, which began in February and continues without resolution, was why Republicans lost.
 Both Vance and Trump Jr. are known to have privately voiced reservations over the ongoing conflict, which many of Trump’s supporters say broke his promise of not entering new foreign wars.
 While Vance said in his post that Trump had also blamed the Iran conflict for GOP losses, Trump only said it was “part of it.”
 Trump has also argued recently that the current situation in Iran is no longer a “war,” even though the US continues to fire on Iranian positions.

 Vance makes his 2028 move
 Analysis by Stephen Collinson 
 SWANTON, OHIO - NOVEMBER 02: U.S. Vice President JD Vance speaks at a campaign rally at Eugene F. Kranz Toledo Express Airport on November 02, 2026 in Swanton, Ohio. Vance is campaigning in Rome, New York and Ohio ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections. (Photo by Tom Brenner/Getty Images) 
 Tom Brenner/Getty Images 
 That didn’t take long.
 Vice President JD Vance posted an extraordinary election post-mortem on X on Wednesday that came across as a transparent attempt to separate himself from Trump and to save his hopes of becoming the Republican nominee in 2028.
 He savaged the GOP’s campaign tactics and its economic messaging and argued that the party was out of touch with the nation’s suffering as costs spiked. All of these strategic calls were made by the president.
 And most bluntly, he wrote: “The reason we lost is the war” – taking aim at the most consequential decision of President Donald Trump’s second term.
 The Vice President came up with four points he said would bring Republican voters back into the fold.
 “1) End the war
 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation
 3) Put America First
 4) Change our relationship to Israel.”
 His critique was clearly not only meant to imply he was all along against the war — which sparked high gas prices that ruined GOP hopes. It was a clear attempt to reach out to the isolationist, Tucker Carlson-wing of what’s left of the MAGA coalition that was attracted by Trump’s ‘no more foreign’ wars mantra in the first place.
 The question after Tuesday’s GOP debacle, however, is whether anyone associated with the unpopular Iran war in any way — and this includes Secretary of State Marco Rubio — would be able to explain it away on the 2028 campaign trail. And will Vance, who, to put it charitably, is prone to political reinvention, be able to pull it off again?
 People were joking yesterday that the 2028 presidential campaign would start Wednesday morning. JD Vance just made it a reality.

 Vance: "The reason we lost is the war"
 By Kit Maher 
 Vice President JD Vance speaks to the media outside Air Force Two on November 2, in Joint Base Andrews, Maryland. 
 Tom Brenner/Getty Images/File 
 Vice President JD Vance is blaming Republicans’ abysmal midterm performance directly on the Iran war.
 “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance, who’s widely expected to be eyeing a 2028 run, said in a lengthy X post Wednesday morning that distanced himself from President Donald Trump and his agenda.
 “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” he said.
 “But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there,” Vance added.
 The vice president said that voters in Trump’s coalition did show up — they just didn’t vote Republican.
 “Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026,” Vance said.
 “There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true,” he added.
 “But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone,” Vance said
 The vice president, citing another pollster, pointed to four things he said could bring those Trump voters back into the fold: end the Iran war, address the high cost of living, put “America First” and change the US relationship to Israel.
 Vance also acknowledged he’d had a bad feeling about Tuesday night. “I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this,” he said.
 Trump has suggested the war played a role but has continued to defend the conflict he started. “I think a part of it was Iran, but at the same time, people understood the importance of what I’ve done with Iran,” he told Fox News in a phone call last night.

 Mexican president celebrates historic Latino wins in Texas and California
 By Uriel Blanco and Max Saltman 
 Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum speaks during the daily morning briefing at Palacio Nacional on June 29, in Mexico City. 
 Jeannette Flores/ObturadorMX/Getty Images 
 Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum told reporters Wednesday that she was “very pleased” with election victories of two prominent Mexican Americans in governors’ in Texas and California.
 “I would like to highlight the victory of two people of Mexican origin: California’s governor-elect (Xavier Becerra) and the governor-elect of Texas (Gina Hinojosa),” Sheinbaum said. “They clearly have ties to their states and their platforms, but also a connection with Mexican men and women.”
 Both victories were historic firsts ; Hinojosa is the first Latina to be elected governor in Texas history, and the first Democrat to win its highest executive office in decades. Becerra , a Democrat, is the first Latino elected governor of California.
 “We are very pleased that Mexican Americans there have this participation and recognition,” Sheinbaum added.

 Cornyn and Talarico spoke by phone Tuesday night
 By Patrick Svitek 
 Republican Sen. John Cornyn speaks to reporters outside the Senate chamber at the US Capitol in Washington, DC on July 30. 
 Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters 
 Republican Sen. John Cornyn spoke by phone on Tuesday night with Democratic Sen.-elect James Talarico, a Cornyn aide told CNN.
 The call came as Talarico was poised to win the race to replace Cornyn in the Senate and end Democrats’ losing streak in Texas. Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton, who unseated Cornyn in the GOP primary.
 Cornyn, who declined to campaign for Paxton, congratulated Talarico on X as the election results were coming in. He said he looked forward to meeting Talarico and helping with the transition.
 Talarico’s campaign confirmed that the two spoke on Tuesday night.

 Jim Jordan announces run for next GOP leader in letter to colleagues
 By Annie Grayer 
 House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan announced his run to lead House Republicans in the minority in a letter to his colleagues obtained by CNN.
 “This is a staggering day for our conference. We are losing colleagues and friends who’ve been valuable members of our conference and leaders in our party,” Jordan wrote.
 “When Americans get knocked down, they pick themselves up and get back to work. Now our Conference must do the same,” Jordan added.
 Jordan argued that Republicans need to go on offense against Democrats over the next two years to win back the majority.
 “For too long, we have operated without a clear plan to survive the hour or the day in front of,” Jordan wrote, making a veiled dig at House Speaker Mike Johnson without naming him.
 Jordan touted his time leading the Judiciary panel as making him uniquely qualified to handle the onslaught of Democratic investigations, referring to himself as “battle-tested.”

 Talarico says Democrats shouldn't focus on "political retribution"
 By Jeff Zeleny 
 Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico speaks at his election night watch party in Austin, Texas on November 3, after delivering a stunning defeat to Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton. 
 Emree Weaver/CNN 
 Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico said Democrats should not be focused on “political retribution” when they assume their Senate majority in January, saying the party has “one last chance” to improve the lives of the American people.
 “They didn’t send us to Washington for political retribution,” Talarico told CNN’s Erin Burnett. “They sent us to Washington to lower costs, to root out corruption, to get this economy back on track and that needs to be our focus.”
 On a crisp sunny morning in Austin, less than 12 hours after accepting victory in his double-digit win over Ken Paxton, Talarico said he had yet to hear directly from his Republican rival. But he said he was pleased to see Paxton’s concession, declaring: “I’m glad that he’s acknowledged the results of the election.”

 When he arrives in Washington, Talarico will become the youngest sitting US senator of the new Congress. He said he intended to work with Democrats across the political spectrum — and Republicans, too — in hopes of making progress on comprehensive immigration reform and more.
 “I’m going to build bridges with all of my 99 colleagues in the US Senate,” Talarico said. “I’m going to build bridges — or at least try to — with President Trump because my mandate is to deliver for working people in my state, to make their lives easier and better.”
 When asked directly about whether Trump should be impeached, Talarico said he would perform his role as a juror, should the House choose to send articles of impeachment to the Senate, just as he did as a member of the Texas House of Representatives when Paxton was impeached.
 “I reviewed every shred of evidence. I listened to every expert and I did my duty accordingly,” Talarico said. “And that’s exactly what I would do in the US Senate.”

 What happens next after all races are called?
 By Catherine Nicholls 
 Voters come and go from the American Legion Post 35 to cast their ballots on Election Day, Tuesday, in Wasilla, Alaska. 
 Lindsey Wasson/AP 
 While it is now clear that Democrats have won control of Congress, some ballots have yet to be counted.
 Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi are still too early to call, while 71 House races have also not yet been projected. It could take weeks for the official results of the election to be known.
 According to the Campaign Legal Center, there are several legal and administrative steps to be taken following an election, namely the canvass, certification, and seating.
 During the canvass, local election officials count all the votes cast in their jurisdiction, including those cast during the early voting period, by mail and on Election Day. Each state then sends a list of its election winners to Congress.
 Before a new Congress convenes in January, elected candidates typically travel to Washington, DC, to take part in new member orientation, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. 
 Following the election, the newly formed Congress will convene in early January, according to the Constitution. 
 A new speaker of the House will be elected by the other members-elect on the first day of Congress, according to the Campaign Legal Center. To be elected speaker, a candidate must win a majority of votes out of all votes cast. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries is expected to be the next House speaker.
 After a speaker is chosen, newly elected senators and all House members are sworn into office and then begin their terms.
 According to the Congressional Research Service , on the first day of Congress, the House also “often adopts resolutions assigning some or many of its Members to committees. This process regularly continues over several more weeks.”
 The majority and minority leaders of the Senate, as well as other party floor officers, are elected “privately by their respective caucuses and not ratified on the floor,” according to the Bipartisan Policy Center.

 What Democratic control of Congress could mean
 By Maureen Chowdhury , Katelyn Polantz and Tierney Sneed 
 Sen.-elect James Talarico and Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa toast with fountain drinks at a Whataburger restaurant following an election night watch party at the Long Center on November 3, in Austin. 
 Brandon Bell/Getty Images 
 Democrats swept races across the country in a colossal midterm victory , delivering a stunning rebuke to President Donald Trump and his policies.
 Democrats were able to capitalize on the president’s historic unpopularity to win significant power to check him for the rest of his term.
 Voters expressed concern over the economy and corruption in polls released ahead of the elections — issues Democrats have vowed to take on.
 Once the new Congress is sworn in, here’s what Democrats’ control of both chambers could mean: 
 Supercharged oversight: Incoming Democratic committee chairs in both chambers will be able to begin putting people and organizations on notice this month. Their power to issue subpoenas begins once the new Congress is seated in January.
 The Senate has much more clearly defined legal power to sue in court to force compliance with its probes. A law passed in 1978 explicitly gives federal courts the authority to order compliance with subpoenas issued by the Senate that meet certain conditions.
 Squire Patton Boggs, a law firm with a prominent Washington lobbying practice, recently gave its clients a list of what may be investigated .
 Those topics include:
 Trump’s construction projects
 Allegations of improper enrichment by Trump and his family members
 The war in Iran
 Immigration enforcement
 The effect of DOGE-prompted cutbacks in 2025 on the federal civil service
 Artificial intelligence
 Affordability
 Trump nominees: The Senate confirms presidential nominees, including Cabinet officials, federal judges and Supreme Court justices. Trump could face an uphill battle getting his nominees confirmed with Democrats holding a majority in the chamber.
 Veto override: Congress can override a president’s veto with a two-thirds vote in both chambers. While Democrats have picked up enough seats to hold solid majorities, they remain far short of the two-thirds threshold.
 Trump told Politico on election night that although he has the right to veto legislation from a Democratic-controlled Congress, he doesn’t “want to be just sitting there for two years vetoing everything.” Trump has previously suggested the opposite, even saying he would become “Mr. Veto.”
 CNN’s Molly English contributed to this report.

 Jim Jordan planning to run for House GOP leader
 By Alayna Treene , Annie Grayer and Sarah Ferris 
 Rep. Jim Jordan speaks to attendees at the 3rd Annual Freedom Fry, hosted by Rep. Russell Fry, on October 26, in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina. 
 Meg Kinnard/AP 
 Congressman Jim Jordan, a fierce Trump ally, is planning to run for House GOP leader now that Speaker Mike Johnson officially cleared the way, two people familiar with the matter tell CNN.
 Jordan was a key Republican leader in the two impeachment proceedings during Trump’s first term, something his allies think will help him in the fight to replace Johnson.
 This sets up a fight for the top GOP leadership spot with Rep. Steve Scalise expected to announce today that he is also running to be the next House Republican leader.
 Rep. August Pfluger will run against Rep. Tom Emmer for the No. 2 leadership spot in the minority – the role of GOP whip — according to a source familiar.
 And Rep. Brian Jack will run for National Republican Congressional Committee chair, according to a source.

 Russian lawmaker Slutsky urges continued negotiations after US midterm elections 
 1:36
 We’re starting to see a flurry of international reaction to the midterm elections swing, as world leaders wake up to the news the Democrats have flipped control of both the House and Senate.
 Here are some of the latest comments:
 Spain: The country’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said the US has voted “against the policies that only impoverish. Against hate. Against machismo. Against climate denialism and against the privileges of the elites.”
 Iran: Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s parliamentary speaker, posted on X that Americans used the elections to say, “NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message.”
 Russia: Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said US President Donald Trump “continues to hold office, and we sincerely hope that he will also continue his peace-making efforts.” Meanwhile, Russian parliamentarian Leonid Slutsky told CNN, “We’ll check the situation. It’s now maybe early for a final conclusion, but it’s not necessary for conclusion. Now Trump is absolutely in (a) negative situation.”
 United Kingdom: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the results give the world “an opportunity now to unite” around the issue of the cost of living. He said he will be calling on fellow world leaders to focus on resolving Russia’s war on Ukraine and the conflict in the Middle East.
 Germany: Defense Minister Boris Pistorius congratulated the Democrats on a “truly remarkable election victory,” noting the Trump administration remains Germany’s point of contact in the US, alongside future talks with Democratic leaders in Congress.
 Norway: Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre told the Reuters news agency the election results were a “powerful political signal about a change of course among American voters.”
 South Africa: President Cyril Ramaphosa said the results will “introduce a new era in world relations,” Reuters reported. “We have seen that the Democrats have taken control of the Senate and of the House, and the people of America have spoken.”
 Poland: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said, “democracy won in America” and echoed Trump’s praise for the Democrats , according to the Reuters news agency. Speaking at a news conference alongside Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis, Tusk also suggested Trump pre-Election Day pledge to “ veto everything ” would be an unwise move.
 Czech Republic: Babis said he hoped Trump would now focus on ending the war in Ukraine and resolving the conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, but that he expected the election would be unlikely to change the course of either.
 CNN’s Vasco Cotovio, Fred Pleitgen and Anna Chernova contributed reporting.

 Democrats take down House GOP's campaign chief in stunning upset
 By Sarah Ferris 
 Rep. Richard Hudson, from North Carolina and chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee, speaks during the second day of the Republican National Committee midterm convention at the American Airlines Center in Dallas, Texas on September 10. 
 Patrick T. Fallon/AFP/Getty Images 
 The biggest upset of the night for House Republicans? The defeat of their own campaign chief, Rep. Richard Hudson in North Carolina.
 Hudson was defeated by Democratic challenger Richard Ojeda in North Carolina’s 9th District, a contest that was barely on either party’s radar until the final days of the race.
 President Donald Trump won the seat by almost 16 points two years ago but Ojeda flipped it with almost no outside spending on his behalf. (National Democrats went up with a late buy to help boost Ojeda last week, as CNN first reported. )
 Ojeda, an Army veteran who served tours in Iraq and Afghanistan, had most recently served as a state legislator in West Virginia. But he moved back to North Carolina in recent years to the same district as the Army base Ft. Bragg, where Ojeda spent part of his own military career.
 Hudson, a close Trump ally, had spent years climbing the ranks of the House GOP since coming to Congress in 2013. As chairman of the National Republican Campaign Committee, Hudson closely tied his party to Trump, hoping to drum up the GOP base.
 For weeks, GOP leaders had brushed off concerns about Hudson’s fate even as a growing number of lawmakers and operatives warned that there was serious voter discontentment in North Carolina.

 Johnson tells staff he's not running for House GOP leader, sources say
 By Manu Raju , Annie Grayer and Sarah Ferris 
 House Speaker Mike Johnson attends a campaign event with Michigan Republicans on October 31, in Sterling Heights, Michigan. 
 Spencer Platt/Getty Images 
 House Speaker Mike Johnson told staff this morning he’s not running for House GOP leader, two sources told CNN, after his party faced devastating losses in Tuesday night’s election.
 One source said Johnson had talked to President Donald Trump about his decision.
 Attention will now shift to a possible matchup between House Majority Leader Steve Scalise and House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan for the GOP leader spot. Other candidates could emerge.
 Scalise has not yet announced whether he will run for minority leader in next week’s caucus-wide vote. But one person familiar with his thinking said he would have “broad support from the conference” and that members have been reaching out to encourage him to run.
 The secret-ballot leadership elections are expected next week.
